body_references.text: The final chapter, [*Deciding With Data and AI*](42-data-driven-decision-making.qmd#separate-prediction-and-valuation), returns to @fig-normative-decision-loop to examine the division of work between AI and people. Better prediction becomes useful when it informs a feasible choice whose consequences matter. The intervening chapters explain why this requires more than a capable model: evidence can be misinterpreted, priorities can remain hidden, authority can silence disagreement, and feedback can fail to correct mistakes. Those lessons provide the basis for designing and evaluating AI-assisted decisions.

In @fig-behavioral-decision-loop, the functions can overlap, recur, become compressed through practice, or be distributed across people and technologies. The arrows show their dependencies and routes of influence.

The distinction between a standard and an explanation now gives the committee a practical task. Use @tbl-hiring-loop to identify where its process is vulnerable, then select a response aimed at that difficulty. Adding another interview will not settle a disagreement about priorities, just as agreeing on priorities will not repair unreliable evidence.

Consider the unfinished sentence **“At the bank, she…”** After a paragraph about fishing, *cast her line* would be a plausible continuation. After a paragraph about opening a savings account, *asked about interest rates* would fit better. The words to be continued are unchanged, but the setting changes what a good answer would be. Like the neighbors around the ambiguous symbol in @fig-context-b13-demonstration, surrounding information guides interpretation. This is useful when context clarifies a task; it becomes consequential when an assumption embedded in the question quietly guides the answer.

In @fig-perception-context-lab, the paired shafts, centre circles, and grey patches are physically identical within each comparison. The surrounding geometry or luminance changes their appearance. Measuring the target can correct the judgment without necessarily turning off the impression.

Look first at the isolated light on the left in @fig-traffic-light-color-context. What color would you call it? Now look at the upper lamp on the right. Both show the same lens, but only the right supplies its familiar setting. Does recognizing the traffic signal make the upper light seem redder?

Before reading the caption, name the animal in @fig-duck-rabbit-context. Then try to find another animal without rotating the image. The challenge is to reorganize the same marks, not discover a second hidden drawing.

The reference class supplies an outside starting point; the causal model explains why the present case might differ. Neither should automatically defeat the other. If only 35% of comparable launches reach that retention target, the illustrative 45% forecast in @tbl-consequence-forecast adds ten percentage points that need a reason. A validated improvement in onboarding might justify an increase; confidence in the team alone does not quantify one. [Chapter 14](14-base-rates-conditional-probability-and-bayesian-updating.qmd#reference-classes-are-judgment-calls) examines the comparison group, and [Chapter 15](15-samples-randomness-regression-and-calibration.qmd#calibration-makes-confidence-answerable) shows how to evaluate forecasts against later outcomes.

In @fig-expectation-loop, one pathway may operate alone, or several may combine. Attention and interpretation can mediate each pathway—for example, symptom monitoring can alter physiology, and a manager's interpretation can alter resource allocation. The key identification question is which pathway changed what followed (Merton, 1948; Harris & Rosenthal, 1985; Kirsch, 1985).

The word “preference” can also hide differences between enjoying an outcome, feeling drawn toward it, judging it worth choosing, and acting from habit. The distinctions in @tbl-value-is-not-one-thing will matter when an action continues even though it brings little pleasure:

Kenrick and colleagues (2010) instead emphasize overlapping systems. @fig-overlapping-motive-systems retains their central point: later-developing motives do not erase earlier ones. The figure uses the broader label **kin care** from later work to include concern for children and other relatives (Neel et al., 2016).

Use @tbl-rationalization-detector to turn a story into claims that can be compared with evidence. A persuasive answer to every question is still a hypothesis; it earns support when it explains observations that plausible rivals do not.

@fig-fast-slow draws on research into controlled and automatic processing (Schneider & Shiffrin, 1977; Shiffrin & Schneider, 1977). The label **System 1** is often used for a family of fast, automatic, intuitive, low-effort, associative, and affective processes; **System 2** groups working-memory-dependent, effortful, rule-guided processes. A single task can recruit several processes, and practice can change which features dominate its performance. These are broad families of processes, not two separate brain structures. Researchers also use **Type 1** and **Type 2** to avoid implying that each family is a single system (Evans & Stanovich, 2013); this book uses the familiar System labels consistently.

The Stroop task makes that conflict visible. In @fig-stroop-interference-lab, name the **ink colour**, rather than read the printed word. Reading is so practiced that a colour name printed in a different colour supplies a competing response before the instructed answer is ready. People are typically slower and more error-prone when controlled attention must resolve this conflict between a fluent but task-irrelevant response and the current goal (Stroop, 1935).
The contrasts in @tbl-04-1 summarize common processing features, not two kinds of person or two fixed locations in the brain. Neither column supplies a guarantee of accuracy.

@fig-anchor-decoy deliberately separates **effect** from **mechanism**. “Insufficient adjustment” is not a complete definition of anchoring: anchor-consistent information can become selectively accessible, and scale use or conversational inferences can also contribute in some tasks (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997). Asymmetric dominance defines the decoy relation (Huber et al., 1982). The diagnostic question is therefore first whether the context changed judgment, and then which mechanism the evidence can distinguish.

@fig-subscription-decoy is memorable because the decoy received no choices, yet its removal changed what people selected. Huber et al. (1982) provide the experimental foundation for this attraction effect.

The hiring case shows why the correction must match the comparison. More careful adjustment cannot create an estimate independent of the anchor; more discussion of the candidate cannot supply a missing work sample. @tbl-14-1 matches the diagnosed problem to a practical change informed by research on debiasing (Larrick, 2004).

In @fig-context-mechanisms, the relevant distinction is what changed: the description, the preceding cue, processing ease, or the result of inaction. The clearest tests of framing hold the other ingredients fixed and compare logically equivalent descriptions.

The rows of @tbl-disease-framing preserve the same final possibilities and probabilities. The first makes a guaranteed rescue focal; the second foregrounds a guaranteed loss. [Chapter 17](17-prospect-theory-gains-and-losses-begin-at-a-reference-point.qmd#the-prospect-theory-model) uses the example to examine how reference points and probability weighting can produce that pattern.

In @fig-assumed-choice-eggs, adding “no egg” restores an option hidden by the second question. “Would you prefer delivery this week or next week?” similarly treats purchase as settled. These are cases of **substantive reframing**: the inquiry changes which options, objectives, or causal accounts receive consideration. They deserve scrutiny even though they are not tests of equivalent numerical descriptions.

That first result could reflect a changed report without a changed memory. A second experiment therefore asked about broken glass one week later. There was none in the film, yet **16 of 50** students previously asked about “smashed” reported seeing it, compared with **7 of 50** asked about “hit” and **6 of 50** controls who received no speed question. @fig-wording-memory-study-redraw keeps the immediate estimate and later report separate.

@fig-fluency-pathway brings together several fluency literatures (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Reber et al., 2004). Ease supplies a signal about our own processing: a readable warning takes less effort to use, and a well-understood explanation is easier to follow. Yet the feeling alone does not reveal its cause. A claim can be fluent because it is understood, because it fits prior belief, because its complexity has been hidden, or simply because it has been repeated. Easy pronunciation has also affected risk judgments in some tasks (Song & Schwarz, 2009).

The two branches in @fig-probability-judgment-map answer the crucial question: who could have produced this positive result? Natural frequencies preserve those nested sets, often making Bayesian reasoning more transparent than isolated percentages (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995). They expose the denominator that the 90% sensitivity figure leaves implicit.

Return to the branch manager. If the bad quarter was two standard deviations below average and the same illustrative correlation of 0.40 applied, the model would predict the next quarter at 0.8 standard deviations below average without any managerial change. That is a visible recovery of 1.2 standard deviations. @fig-regression-conditional-shrinkage shows the corresponding geometry. The recovery can be real while its attribution to the rescue plan remains unproven. Compare the branch with similarly troubled branches, examine several earlier periods, and identify which changes the manager actually introduced. That makes room for a managerial effect while accounting for the recovery that might have happened anyway.
Each requires a different comparison, as @tbl-confidence-calibration shows. Asking a confident person to “think harder” supplies none of them.

The **planning fallacy** illustrates how optimistic forecasts can affect a project: people often construct an inside-view story of the steps that should occur while underweighting delays observed in similar projects (Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Underestimating the time a task needs can express overestimation of what one can accomplish in that time; an unduly narrow completion window also expresses overprecision. Planning fallacy is therefore an application, rather than a fourth form alongside those in @tbl-confidence-calibration. The **outside view** begins with a reference class and then adjusts only for differences that are genuinely predictive (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993; Lovallo & Kahneman, 2003).
@fig-risky-decision-map shows the first calculation: the lottery’s average utility lies below the utility of its average wealth.
@fig-experience-rare-event-sampling isolates the sampling mechanism. The following sections examine how selective exposure, stopping, and memory shape the experienced record.
@fig-well-being-six-lenses makes the central discipline visible: **do not move between measures without saying so**. A decision can look successful through one lens and costly through another.

Having followed the job through prediction, choice, experience, and reflection, use @tbl-well-being-targets to keep the questions separate. A strong answer in one row cannot silently stand in for the others.
The distinctions can now be collected in @tbl-three-strategic-lenses. Choose a lens by the question it answers: a stable profile, a player’s reasoning, or change in a population.

@tbl-cooperation-mechanisms compares features of an interaction that can change the incentive to cooperate. These features can coexist: a repeated relationship can also have a reputation system and formal enforcement. Use the comparison to identify what would change the prediction, rather than treating every cooperative act as evidence of generosity.

Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler (1986) asked separate samples of respondents to judge market practices. @fig-fairness-entitlements-redraw shows four selected historical vignettes. The car questions hold the size of the price increase at $200 but vary its relation to list price: one adds a surcharge above list, while the other removes a discount below list.[^ch25-fairness-vignettes]
Use @tbl-22-1 to audit the cue behind an apparent consensus before treating the consensus as additional evidence.

For Lena’s team, the next step is to distinguish the causes hidden by the shared silence. @fig-silence-mechanisms previews five pathways; the sections that follow show why each needs a different safeguard.
Use @tbl-group-failure-pathways to select the next observation and action. Several pathways may coexist, so record what each safeguard is expected to change.

The [previous chapter](28-authority-groupthink-and-shared-responsibility.qmd#chapter-28-start) examined how authority can keep concerns out of a decision. Here we examine a prior problem: recognizing a concern when people express it differently from what we expect. @fig-culture-meaning-map traces how the same observable action acquires different meanings along the way.

Evidence constrains the models that deserve belief. But a visible pattern may fit several accounts: steady growth, acceleration, or an approaching plateau. In @fig-model-underdetermination, all three curves fit the observations so far, but a later observation of 44 favors the plateau. These are synthetic data: the point is to identify an observation that could distinguish the accounts before deciding which story to tell.

@tbl-25-barriers separates objections that another statistic can address from concerns requiring a change in governance, training, or workload. Listening may reveal a defect in the proposal rather than in its presentation.

The five-part route in @fig-story-update turns this change of explanation into a writing template. Ask what the protagonist believed, what challenged that belief, and what further evidence would justify changing it. Sara’s discovery of a previously unreported risk gives her a reason to investigate the meeting process; it does not yet establish which part of that process caused the silence.

Build a **one-page STORY brief** for one research claim, policy, product, leadership request, or negotiation proposal. The single brief contains five rows: Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons, and Yes. In the Reasons row, identify the pivotal claim, classify it using @tbl-27-claim-evidence, give the strongest available evidence and comparison, state the uncertainty, and name what the evidence does not establish. At the bottom, answer three audit questions: Is any case presented as representative without a denominator? Can the audience meaningfully decline or revise the requested action? Which one sentence should be weakened or removed if the evidence is insufficient? Use the completed brief to deliver a 90-second message. Peer feedback identifies one unsupported inferential jump and one concrete repair. Working alone, mark every claim that needs outside evidence, check the pivotal one against its source, and revise the brief before delivering it again.

The manager sees a late section and wants to prevent another missed deadline. The colleague hears a judgment about reliability and wants the accusation corrected. Treating either account as the whole problem would leave the other concern unanswered. Start by separating the event, your own felt impact, and your interpretation. @tbl-29-2 is a self-check before listening: it helps identify which parts of your account the other person needs an opportunity to correct.
@fig-conversation-repair brings the conversation back to three tasks: describe the event, check what it meant, and agree on the next action. Each needs an answer from both people.

A Pareto frontier is the set of Pareto-efficient agreements under those specifications. The feasible set may be discrete, nonconvex, or only partly known. The two axes in @fig-pareto represent each party's own value measure. Each axis is interpreted in that party's own units.[^ch37-value-units]

Begin with @tbl-37-package-scores: identify the dominated package and compare each remaining package with the stated walk-away scores. Then use the opening supplier case to draft three more realistic packages. The reported case does not supply complete valuations or BATNAs, so label any scoring assumptions you introduce and identify the information needed to replace them. In pairs, assign roles and exchange rankings or conditional package preferences before revealing exact limits. Working alone, write two plausible priority maps and the question that would distinguish them. Revise one package after that check.

Choose **no more than one** optional module from @tbl-agreement-module-routing. State the diagnosed problem that justifies it and add only the information that module requires—for example, two or three sincere packages for unclear priorities, one measurable contingent term for forecast disagreement, or one explicit escalation rule for process failure. If no module is justified, record “none.” Multiple packages, full contingent-contract drafting, independent audits, detailed mediation or arbitration clauses, and multi-shock testing belong in an advanced agreement-design file, not in the minimum exercise.
Use @fig-agreement-design to check package sincerity, measurement and incentives, protection of the signed agreement, and governance. These conditions determine which tool fits the negotiation.

@fig-behavior-design brings together several ideas. The Fogg Behavior Model describes motivation, ability, and a cue for action converging at a behavioral moment; its earlier term “trigger” became “prompt” in later presentations (Fogg, 2009, 2020). COM-B treats capability, opportunity, and motivation as interacting conditions, with feedback from behavior (Michie et al., 2011). Research on implementation intentions, habits, and behavior-change maintenance supports planning, feedback, and preparation for obstacles (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006; Kwasnicka et al., 2016; Wood & Rünger, 2016). A lapse or harm may reveal a cue, constraint, support need, or goal that needs reconsideration.
Choose one mild, real behavior and complete the one-page record in @tbl-behavior-design-workflow:
3. **Redesign:** change one decisive point. Choose no more than one primary tool from @tbl-21-1 and state exactly what will be different in the environment or response.

An instruction to “ignore the chair’s opinion” comes too late if members have already heard it. The process must capture their assessments earlier and preserve them for review. @fig-structured-judgment-pipeline groups that work into six stages. The checklist below expands two of them: establish a baseline before gathering judgments, and challenge the emerging conclusion before committing. Use this as the chapter’s main workflow; the later audits and record templates help carry out particular steps.

@fig-schelling-emergence applies that standard. In one seeded Schelling-style teaching run, agents move only when fewer than one-third of their occupied neighbours share their group and choose a vacancy satisfying that threshold. The average same-group-neighbour share rises from 0.48 to 0.68.
Keep the record in @tbl-literature-search-record as you work. It lets a reader understand the scope and lets you recover a decision you might otherwise forget.

The three papers in @tbl-savings-review-example are a deliberately selected teaching example, adapted from the lecture. They illustrate how studies can perform different jobs in a synthesis; they are not an exhaustive or current review of saving arrangements.

Choose one claim from the book or current media. Place it in @fig-claim-to-design-pipeline. State the question, construct, measure, comparison, estimand, and final sentence. Mark the weakest arrow. Then propose the smallest feasible redesign that would strengthen that link. If the redesign cannot support the original claim, narrow the claim.

Follow the two forks in @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment. The first determines who enters the evaluation; the second determines which condition those participants are assigned to. The control group is part of the evaluation sample and must be followed for outcomes. People outside the evaluation are not that control group. The figure shows one possible design: a trial can use random assignment without random sampling, as in the volunteer example above, while requiring a separate argument about generalization.

The markets receiving no offers were deliberately included and measured as **pure controls**. They are different from the people outside the evaluation in @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment. Higher-level assignment, buffer areas, or network measurement may also help, but none should be treated as proof that interference has disappeared. State whose outcome depends on whose treatment and whether the study estimates an individual gain, an effect on others, or a broader policy effect.

Suppose the clinic establishes that its new reminder improves attendance. A neighboring clinic wants to adopt it, but serves patients with different needs and uses a different booking system. The original comparison cannot by itself tell that clinic what to expect. The sampling step in @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment supports inference to a defined population; extending the result to a different setting requires examining what else has changed.

2. Trace a patient through @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment. Explain how being outside the evaluation differs from assignment to its control group, and when household assignment might be preferable.

The three panels in @fig-participant-flow-threats distinguish problems that are easily collapsed into “dropout.” **Noncompliance** concerns treatment receipt, **attrition** concerns missing outcomes after loss to follow-up, and **spillovers or interference** concern effects on other people. They can occur together, but they change different parts of the comparison. The final panel states the starting point for analysis: retain original assignment when estimating the intention-to-treat effect, then address the assumptions threatened by missing outcomes and interference.

@tbl-research-reactivity is a set of design questions, not a claim that all six effects occur in every study. A systematic review found highly varied evidence under the Hawthorne label, with substantial uncertainty about mechanisms and magnitudes (McCambridge et al., 2014). More specifically, Zwane and colleagues (2011) randomly varied survey exposure across five field studies: surveys increased use of health products in three studies, but the two microlending studies did not detect changes in borrowing. Measurement can matter without having one predictable effect everywhere.

Each stage in @fig-selected-evidence-pipeline changes what readers can know. Preregistration records a plan; open code lets others check the calculation; replication collects new evidence. Their usefulness depends on the problem at that stage.

Do not vote “true” or “false.” Map the case onto @fig-selected-evidence-pipeline. Identify the uncertainty introduced at design, data, analysis, publication, and replication. Then propose: (a) the next study, (b) the cumulative claim that is warranted now, and (c) one institutional change that would have made the evidence easier to interpret.

@fig-selected-literature-simulation isolates one mechanism. The generator uses independent normal-outcome studies with true effect 0.20 standard deviations, outcome variance 1, 50 observations per arm, and seed 20260830. A known-variance, two-sided z test with alpha .05 gives each difference in means standard error 0.20 and theoretical power 17.0%. The significance-only rule makes 328 of 2,000 studies visible; their mean estimate is 0.490, about 2.5 times the true effect, and four have the wrong sign. The deterministic generator is `scripts/build_methods_appendix_figures.py`; its study-level output and parameter record are preserved in `figures/source/selected-literature-simulation.csv` and `.json`.
